title: Incorporate basic concepts of sustainable farming systems into practical farm activities

lessons.title: Sustainable farming concepts
lessons.html:
The three pillars

A sustainable farming system balances three things:

  • Environmental: soil, water, veld and biodiversity stay healthy or improve.
  • Economic: the farm stays profitable and can pay its bills and workers.
  • Social: workers and communities are treated fairly and safely.

A farm that makes money but destroys its soil is not sustainable. Nor is a farm that protects nature but goes bankrupt.

Key concepts

  • Soil health: a living soil with organic matter, structure and soil organisms. Practices: minimum tillage, cover crops, crop rotation, compost.
  • Water efficiency: using less water per unit produced, through scheduling, drip irrigation, mulching and rainwater harvesting.
  • Nutrient cycling: returning manure and crop residues to the land; fertilising based on soil tests rather than habit.
  • Integrated pest management (IPM): preventing pests with resistant cultivars, rotation and natural enemies, scouting regularly, and using chemicals only when thresholds are reached.
  • Biodiversity: keeping natural vegetation, hedgerows and wetlands that support pollinators and predators.
  • Veld and grazing management: matching stocking rate to carrying capacity and resting camps.
  • Energy and waste: reducing diesel use, using solar where possible, recycling and disposing safely.

Conservation agriculture

Conservation agriculture is promoted widely in South African grain areas. It rests on three principles: minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop rotation or diversity. It helps protect soil from erosion and can improve water infiltration.

The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 sets the legal framework for protecting soil, water and vegetation on farmland.

lessons.title: Putting sustainability into daily farm work
lessons.html:
Turning concepts into actions

As a supervisor, you translate these ideas into the tasks your team does every day.

In crop lands

  • Leave crop residue on the surface instead of burning it.
  • Plant cover crops (such as oats, vetch or radish mixes) in fallow periods where planned.
  • Follow contour lines for planting and keep contour banks maintained.
  • Scout fields weekly and record pest levels so spraying is only done when needed.
  • Calibrate sprayers and spreaders so the correct rate is applied.

In irrigation

  • Check soil moisture before irrigating (probe, tensiometer or the feel method).
  • Fix leaks and blocked emitters the same day.
  • Irrigate at cooler times to reduce evaporation.

With livestock

  • Move animals according to the grazing plan.
  • Report overgrazed or eroded areas and bush encroachment.
  • Keep animals out of riverbanks and wetlands where fenced off.
  • Collect manure for compost where possible.

Waste and chemicals

  • Triple-rinse empty chemical containers, puncture them and return them to the store for approved disposal.
  • Store fuel and chemicals in bunded, locked stores away from water.
  • Separate recyclables from general waste.

People

  • Give clear instructions and training, including why a practice matters.
  • Provide PPE and make sure it is used.
  • Encourage workers to report problems and ideas.

Measuring progress

Keep records: yields, water use, inputs, rainfall, grazing days per camp, and soil test results over time. Records show whether practices are working and justify the investment.

Key points

  • Sustainability balances environment, economy and people.
  • Conservation agriculture: minimum disturbance, soil cover, rotation.
  • Use IPM and scouting so chemicals are only used when needed.
  • Irrigate based on soil moisture and fix leaks quickly.
  • Record results to show which practices work.
